interactive.title: A slope tracker
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens with two graphs, one above the other, sharing the same x across. The top graph is the speeding boat from the last two lessons, f(x) = x² metres after x seconds, where x² means x × x. A point P can be dragged along the curve, and the tangent at P rides with it, with a readout of its slope in m per s, the number the chords from P settle on. The bottom graph plots that slope upwards: wherever P goes, it drops a dot at the same x, as high as the slope there. At 1, 2, 3 and 4 s the slopes are 2, 4, 6 and 8 m per s, and dragging P all the way leaves a trail of dots along a straight line through zero that rises 2 for every 1 across, f′(x) = 2x. Middle screens show a growing square: a square of side x whose side grows by a small step h, so the new square is the old one plus two strips, each x by h, and a corner h by h. A slider shrinks h, and a readout adds the strips and the corner and divides by h, giving 2x + h, which settles on 2x; at x = 3 it reads 7, 6.5, 6.1 and 6.01 as h goes 1, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01. Later screens drop the boat and run the plain curve y = x² from −3 to 3, falling on the left, where its dots carry on along the same line below the axis; then a straight line, y = 4x, whose dots sit on a flat line at 4; then the curve y = x² − 2x, whose dots trace 2x − 2. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is shown going wrong on the graphs.
interactive.ignores: The boat's rule is an example rule, chosen so the numbers come out exactly. The trail on the bottom graph is made of the slopes at the places P visits, joined up between them. The square's step h is drawn large enough to see the strips and the corner. A side cannot be below zero, so the square only pictures x above zero, but the working (x + h)² = x² + 2xh + h² holds for any x, which is why the line of dots carries on to the left.

explain.text:
The derivative is the rate at an instant worked out at every point at once, and the answers make a new function of their own. Last lesson the speeding boat, f(x) = x² metres after x seconds, was doing 6 m per s at 3 s. Do the same at other moments and each gives one rate: 2 m per s at 1 s, 4 at 2 s, 6 at 3 s and 8 at 4 s, each the number its chords settle on. Plot each rate as a dot on a second graph below, at the same x, with the rate going up instead of the distance. The dots line up on a straight line through zero that rises 2 for every 1 across, so at x seconds the boat is doing 2x metres per second. That rule is a function in its own right, the [[derivative]] of f, written f′(x) and read 'f dash of x' (many books say 'f prime'). Like any function, it takes a number, x, and gives one back, here the slope of f at x. It gives the rate at each point of f where there is one.[^2] For f(x) = x², f′(x) = 2x.

Four dots on a line suggest the rule, and a square shows why it holds. Since x² is x × x, picture it as the area of a square of side x. Make the side longer by a small step h. The new square is the old one plus two thin strips, each x long and h wide, plus a tiny corner h by h, the same area model you used for brackets in Linear equations. So the area grows by 2xh + h². On the graph of y = x², moving from x to x + h raises y by exactly that growth, so the chord between them has Δy = 2xh + h² over Δx = h. Divide each piece by h: each strip, x by h, leaves x, and the corner, h by h, leaves h, so the slope is 2x + h. Shrink h and the h left over shrinks with it, so the slope settles on 2x. At x = 3 the chord's slope is 6 + h, which is why, in every column of last lesson's table, the amount above 6 was the gap itself: a gap of 1 gave 7 and a gap of 0.5 gave 6.5. Working out a derivative is called [[differentiating]], and textbooks call doing it from chords like this working from first principles.

Keep the number and the rule apart. f′(3) = 6 is one number, the slope at x = 3, while f′(x) = 2x is the whole rule, which gives a slope for any x you put in. f′(3) = 6 does not put the curve, or its tangent, through (3, 6): the curve is at (3, 9), and the 6 is how steeply it climbs there, the height of the dot on the graph below. The rule holds on both sides of zero, because multiplying out (x + h)² gives x² + 2xh + h² for any x, not only for a square's side. The plain curve y = x² falls to the left of zero as x grows, so its slopes there are below zero: f′(−2) = −4, and the dots carry on along the same line below the axis. At x = 0 the curve is flat at the bottom and f′(0) = 0. Other functions have their own derivatives. A straight line has the same slope everywhere, so its derivative is that slope at every x, a flat line on the graph below: for the steady boat, f(x) = 4x, it is 4 m per s at every moment. For f(x) = x² − 2x the derivative is f′(x) = 2x − 2.[^1] In engineering and physics the same rule is often written dy/dx = 2x.[^3] At a sharp corner, where the slopes from the left and from the right settle on different values, there is no derivative at that point.[^4] **The derivative f′(x) is the rule that gives the rate of change of f at each point where it has one, and for y = x² it is 2x.[^2]**

analogy.text: A van's mileometer and its speedometer describe the same journey. Note the mileometer every moment and you get a distance graph; note the speedometer every moment and you get a second graph, the speed at each moment. The speed graph is the derivative of the distance graph: at every moment it says how steeply the distance is climbing, as the dots on the lower graph do for y = x².
analogy.breaks: A speedometer reads speed from the turning wheels or gearbox, not from the mileometer, while the derivative is worked out exactly from the distance rule. And a mileometer normally only counts up, so its speed graph never goes below zero; a derivative goes below zero wherever the quantity falls, as on the left of y = x².

practice.text:
- Pick a few values of x and find the rate at each, the number its chords settle on.
- Plot each rate as a dot above its x on a second graph, with the rate going up.
- Look for the rule the dots follow, and test it at a value you have not plotted.
- To be sure, work from first principles: write the growth f(x + h) − f(x), divide it by h, and see what it settles on as h shrinks.
- Use the rule: put a value of x in to get the rate there, in the y unit per x unit.

**Rules of thumb:** f(3) is a height and f′(3) is a slope; keep them apart. Where the curve climbs, f′ is above zero; where it falls, below zero; where it is flat, zero. A straight line's derivative is its slope, the same at every x.

**Worked example:** A square hatch of side x metres has an area of x² square metres. At what rate does its area grow as the side grows, when the side is 1.5 m? The derivative of x² is 2x, so the rate is 2 × 1.5 = 3 m² per metre of side. Check with a chord: a side of 1.6 m gives 2.56 m², which is 0.31 m² more than 2.25 m², and 0.31 ÷ 0.1 = 3.1, above 3 by the step itself, as 2x + h says.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading the height as the slope. At 1.5 m the area is 2.25 m², but it is growing at 3 m² per metre of side.
- Reading f′(−1) = −2 as the point (−1, −2). It is the slope at x = −1; y = x² is at (−1, 1) there.
- Forgetting to divide by h. The growth 2xh + h² is an amount, not a rate.
- Writing the derivative of 4x as 4x. A straight line's slope is the same everywhere, so it is 4.

interactive.html:
Two graphs sharing one x: above, an example speeding boat, f(x) = x² metres after x seconds; below, its slope at each moment.

Every slope and dot here is worked out from each screen's own rule.
interactive.title: A slope tracker
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the tangent's slope at each point dropping a dot on the graph below, and the dots tracing the straight line f′(x) = 2x, when you drag the point along y = x².

checks.label: The derivative function gives the derivative of a function at each point where it is defined: on every graph, each dot below sits straight under the place P visited, as high as the number the chords there settle on from either side, and the tangent through P has that slope

The function f(x) = x squared – 2x is graphed as is its derivative f′(x) = 2x − 2: on the last screen, answered, every dot below reads 2x − 2 at its x, and the tangent at x = 3 climbs 4 for every 1 across

From the rules, by hand: x² is 1, 4, 9 and 16 m at 1 to 4 s, with slopes 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 m per s at 1 to 5 s; chords from 4 s read 0.81 ÷ 0.1 = 8.1 and 0.0801 ÷ 0.01 = 8.01; the square of side 3 gives 7, 6.5, 6.1 and 6.01; side 5 grown by 0.1 gives strips 1, corner 0.01, 1.01 and 10.1; y = x² has slopes −4, −2, 0 and 2 at −2, −1, 0 and 1; 4x and 3x have slopes 4 and 3 everywhere; a 20 cm plate grows at 40 cm² per cm; x² − 2x is 3 at 3, with slope 4; and the screens' sentences quote these same values

Swept along the whole boat graph, the dots lie on a straight line through zero that rises 2 for every 1 across: every dot and every point of the trail below reads 2x, the rise step reads 2, and the working says f′(x) = 2x

The growing square of side 3: at every stop of the slider the old square is drawn 3 across, the strips h wide (never under 8 units, so they show), and the table and working give the growth (3 + h)² − 9 = 2 × 3 × h + h × h divided by h, which is 6 + h

Every puzzle offers three different answers and accepts only the right one; each wrong answer is the slip it stands for: 16 m and 8.01 m per s against 8 m per s; 25 m and 7 m per s against 10 m per s; 1.01 and 10 against 10.1; the point (−1, −2) and a slope of 2 against a slope of −2; 3x and 0 against 3; 400 cm² and 20 cm² per cm against 40 cm² per cm; 3 and 6 against 4

Before an answer no puzzle shows it: no tangent, no dot at P, nothing red, and the working ends in a question mark; a right answer shows its value with nothing red, and every wrong answer shows its slip in red
Dragging P keeps it on a half step inside the axes, and the trail joins only half steps P has passed
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 1.3 s

applied.problem: A square's side cannot be below zero, so the square only shows why f′(x) = 2x holds for x above zero, yet the text says it shows every x and later asserts the rule holds on both sides of zero with no reason; the algebra (x + h)² = x² + 2xh + h² is what covers negative x.
'Only ever counts up' is too absolute: some older mechanical mileometers turned back when the vehicle was driven in reverse; 'normally' keeps the point (speed never goes below zero) true.
